name: Pattern Steps
topics_techniques_covered: number_series: infer a repeating, growing, alternating, or interleaved quantity rule and supply the next term
number_series: continue early pictorial quantity sequences with dots, groups, and step-built figures before numerals appear
pattern_completion: extend repeating and growing patterns across figural and quantitative representations
pattern_completion: coordinate two changing features or two interleaved rules at the upper-band ceiling
one_liner: The child chooses the next quantity or figure that continues a stepping pattern.
interaction: A left-to-right row shows 3-7 quantity or figure cards followed by one glowing empty step and 4-6 answer cards. The child taps an answer card to snap it into the empty step, may tap another to swap, and taps a large pulse button to submit. K-1 cards use only dots, grouped objects, or built figures - never written numerals - and every band answers by tap, not typing.
self_teach: In a wordless ghost-hand animation lasting under 10 seconds, three steps gain one dot each; the hand taps the four-dot card, it snaps into place, and the path lights forward. One unscored warm-up then presents an AB dot pattern, giving a green pulse for the continuation or a gentle shake followed by the demonstrated answer before scored items begin.

learning_science.principle: Learning trajectories align task demands with developing mathematical thought
learning_science.why: Pattern reasoning can progress from perceptually available repetitions to coordinated quantitative rules without changing the response shell.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The generator climbs a fixed trajectory from repeating dots to growing quantities, alternating changes, and finally interleaved or dual-feature rules.
learning_science.source: Clements, D. H., & Sarama, J. (2004). Learning trajectories in mathematics education. Mathematical Thinking and Learning, 6(2), 81-89.

learning_science.principle: Overlapping-waves theory treats strategy variability and increasingly adaptive strategy choice as central to cognitive development
learning_science.why: Children may continue a series by perceptual matching, counting differences, or coordinating multiple rules, and those strategies carry more information than correctness alone.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Distractors instantiate repeat-the-last, copy-the-surface, wrong-step-size, and single-rule-only strategies so error type and rule dimensionality remain interpretable.
learning_science.source: Siegler, R. S. (1996). Emerging Minds: The Process of Change in Children's Thinking. Oxford University Press.

learning_science.principle: Cognitive load theory calls for removing extraneous demands from novel reasoning tasks
learning_science.why: Reading directions or decoding notation would mask induction, especially for pre-readers.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use one visible sequence, large answer cards, no text, no timer pressure, and dots or figures at K-1 so working memory is reserved for the rule.
learning_science.source: Sweller, J., van Merrienboer, J. J. G., & Paas, F. (2019). Cognitive architecture and instructional design: 20 years later. Educational Psychology Review, 31(2), 261-292.

tail_precision_rationale: M-DIFFREACH locates the hardest generated rule family the child can continue, while M-RULEID records whether one, two, or more coordinated changes were successfully integrated. Rule-keyed M-ERRTYPE distinguishes a near-ceiling single-rule continuation from repetition or random choice, and M-RTFIRST captures deliberate encoding before selection without rewarding speed. Across an escalating run, M-LEARNRATE shows how quickly the child moves from visible repetitions to unfamiliar alternating and interleaved structures, adding dynamic evidence to M-ACC at the gifted cut.
age_rationale: K-1 receives 3-4 card sequences made only of large dots, object groups, and simple built figures, avoiding reading, numeral recognition, and fine dragging. Grades 2-3 may add small numerals paired with quantity pictures and one changing rule; grades 4-5 coordinate alternating or multiplicative growth; grades 6-8 reach interleaved, recursive-looking, and two-feature rules without algebra notation. Large tap targets and a single snap slot keep motor demand stable across bands.

adaptive.content_range: AB dot and plus-one quantity patterns at K-1 through long-gap, alternating, multiplicative, interleaved, and two-feature quantitative series at the 6-8 ceiling
difficulty_levers: sequence length and amount of visible evidence
rule family from repeat to additive to multiplicative to alternating or interleaved
step size and presence of a changing step size
quantity representation from dots or figures to supported numerals
adaptive.notes: A rule grammar can generate unlimited valid sequences, verify a unique continuation, and produce distractors from named misconceptions. Escalate after success across rule family and rule count until repeated failure, while retaining perceptually matched parallel clones for consistency.

engagement_hook: Each correct continuation builds the next glowing stone in a path; harder rules make the path change shape and unlock visually richer stepping trails.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Long rows can become a visual-memory test, so keep all terms visible and cap row length by band; dot size, spacing, and color must not accidentally reveal the rule; color can never be the only changing attribute; numeral recognition is avoided at K-1 and visually supported later; large tap cards remove fine-motor demands; do not score raw speed because careful induction is expected.

name: Number Web
topics_techniques_covered: numeric_matrix: complete 2x2 and 3x3 quantity matrices whose rows and columns obey generated arithmetic relations
number_analogies: infer the transformation from one quantity pair and apply it to a second pair in a 2x2 relation
quantitative_reasoning_mixed: integrate magnitude, grouping, comparison, and multi-relation number reasoning without written operation strings
one_liner: The child finds the quantity tile that completes every connection in a number web.
interaction: A 2x2 analogy or 3x3 web has one glowing empty cell and 4-6 candidate quantity tiles. Quantities are shown as segmented bars, grouped dots, or numerals paired with a magnitude strip; relation arrows animate only during the demo and carry no labels. The child taps one tile to place it, may swap it, and taps the central web button to submit, with no typing or reading.
self_teach: A wordless ghost hand traces a two-dot tile becoming a four-dot tile across the top row, traces the same connection from three dots to the empty cell, and taps the six-dot answer; the completed web glows, all in under 10 seconds. One unscored single-relation 2x2 warm-up follows with corrective animation before scored items.

learning_science.principle: Relational complexity theory predicts that reasoning load rises with the number of relations coordinated at once
learning_science.why: The intended ceiling is not larger printed numbers but binding multiple row and column constraints simultaneously.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Difficulty escalates from one binary input-output relation in a 2x2 to two or three co-acting row and column relations in a 3x3, and each foil violates a known subset.
learning_science.source: Halford, G. S., Wilson, W. H., & Phillips, S. (1998). Processing capacity defined by relational complexity. Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 21(6), 803-831.

learning_science.principle: Process analyses of matrix reasoning emphasize rule induction and goal management over surface appearance
learning_science.why: A quantitative matrix should reveal which relation was induced rather than reward familiarity with a fixed puzzle layout.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Generate items from an explicit relation grammar and key distractors to omissions, reversals, or misapplication of individual rules.
learning_science.source: Carpenter, P. A., Just, M. A., & Shell, P. (1990). What one intelligence test measures: A theoretical account of the processing in the Raven Progressive Matrices Test. Psychological Review, 97(3), 404-431.

learning_science.principle: Grounded representations can support quantitative reasoning when formal symbols are difficult to comprehend
learning_science.why: Magnitude bars and grouped quantities let children reason about the transformation without first translating operation notation.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Every numeral is paired with a proportional visual magnitude representation, and operations are expressed by example pairs rather than written symbols.
learning_science.source: Koedinger, K. R., & Nathan, M. J. (2004). The real story behind story problems: Effects of representations on quantitative reasoning. Journal of the Learning Sciences, 13(2), 129-164.

tail_precision_rationale: M-RULEID and rule-keyed M-ERRTYPE turn a hard web into relation-level evidence: a child satisfying two of three constraints is distinguishable from one applying an unrelated rule. M-DIFFREACH identifies the maximum matrix size, relation family, and simultaneous rule count solved, while M-RTFIRST captures time spent encoding the full web before acting. M-LEARNRATE across novel relation families helps separate rapid abstraction from practiced arithmetic, and M-ACC anchors the adaptive estimate.
age_rationale: The task begins in grade 2 because coordinating an analogy across two quantity pairs requires more relational control than the K-1 catalog should assume. Grades 2-3 use 2x2 webs, grouped dots, bars, and small whole-number transformations; grades 4-5 add 3x3 rows and columns; grades 6-8 coordinate inverse, composition, partition, and cross-row rules. No prose or algebra notation is required, and large tap tiles avoid fine-motor demands.

adaptive.content_range: single-relation 2x2 quantity analogies with concrete magnitude tiles through 3x3 webs requiring several co-acting additive, multiplicative, partition, inverse, or composed relations
difficulty_levers: one to three simultaneous row and column relations
relation family and number of transformation steps
missing-cell position and amount of redundant evidence
distractors violating one versus several constraints
adaptive.notes: Generate a complete latent web first, mask one cell, and solve it independently to guarantee uniqueness; derive foils from specific rule violations. Adaptive escalation prioritizes relation count over arithmetic size so the ceiling remains quantitative reasoning rather than calculation fluency.

engagement_hook: The web behaves like a circuit: the correct quantity closes every glowing connection and sends a pulse around the grid.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Matrix familiarity, numeral fluency, and visual clutter can contaminate performance; use the ghost-hand warm-up, pair symbols with magnitudes, and keep connectors sparse. Arithmetic facts must stay easy relative to the target relation count. Do not use color as the sole code, keep targets large, permit unhurried inspection, and calibrate 2x2 versus 3x3 layouts separately.

name: Machine Rule
topics_techniques_covered: pattern_completion: infer a number machine input-output transformation from examples and predict a new output
number_analogies: transfer the same quantitative change from demonstrated input-output pairs to a novel input
arithmetic_reasoning: compose, reverse, or condition a quantity transformation without requiring a written equation
one_liner: The child watches what a machine does to quantities and chooses what it will make next.
interaction: Two to four example trays show an input quantity entering a machine and an output quantity emerging; a final input enters and the output tray remains empty. The child taps one of 4-6 output tiles and then the machine's large start button. K-1 uses countable objects and dots only, later bands may pair numerals with bars, and no child types a numeral.
self_teach: In an under-10-second wordless demo, a tray of two stars enters, four stars roll out, then three enter and six roll out; the ghost hand taps the matching output for one final example and the machine cheers. One unscored warm-up with a visible add-one transformation follows, with a corrective replay if needed.

learning_science.principle: Grounded representations can elicit reliable quantitative strategies before formal symbolism is fluent
learning_science.why: A visible machine acting on object quantities makes input-output structure comprehensible without operation words or algebra notation.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Present transformations through repeated concrete pairs and quantity bars, reserving written numerals as a redundant representation rather than a prerequisite.
learning_science.source: Koedinger, K. R., & Nathan, M. J. (2004). The real story behind story problems: Effects of representations on quantitative reasoning. Journal of the Learning Sciences, 13(2), 129-164.

learning_science.principle: Worked examples should fade smoothly into independent problem solving
learning_science.why: The child must learn the novel shell without being taught the scored rule.
learning_science.concrete_decision: The ghost hand fully solves a structurally simple demonstration, the warm-up requires the child's selection with feedback, and all scored machine rules are new and feedback-free.
learning_science.source: Renkl, A., & Atkinson, R. K. (2003). Structuring the transition from example study to problem solving in cognitive skill acquisition. Educational Psychologist, 38(1), 15-22.

learning_science.principle: Learning trajectories support progress from concrete actions to coordinated mathematical transformations
learning_science.why: The same machine can move from one visible change to composed and conditional rules while remaining intuitive.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Escalate from copy, add, remove, or duplicate quantities to inverse, two-stage, alternating, and input-dependent transformations only after mastery evidence.
learning_science.source: Clements, D. H., & Sarama, J. (2004). Learning trajectories in mathematics education. Mathematical Thinking and Learning, 6(2), 81-89.

tail_precision_rationale: M-DIFFREACH records the most complex transformation solved, and M-RULEID distinguishes a one-step rule from successful coordination of two stages or a condition. M-ERRTYPE identifies copy-input, apply-only-one-stage, reverse-rule, and additive-for-multiplicative errors, preserving near-miss information at the ceiling. M-LEARNRATE is especially useful because every run introduces unfamiliar machine rules: the rate at which a child uses examples to climb the ladder adds learning-potential evidence beyond M-ACC, while M-RTFIRST indexes rule inspection before response.
age_rationale: K-1 receives countable dot or object inputs, one visible operation, totals within a small range, and oversized tap tiles, with no numerals or reading. Grades 2-3 add larger grouped quantities and inverse changes; grades 4-5 add two-stage machines; grades 6-8 add alternating or input-conditioned transformations represented entirely by examples. The interaction never requires typing, fine dragging, operation vocabulary, or algebraic symbols.

adaptive.content_range: copy, add-one, remove-one, double, or split concrete quantities at K-1 through inverse, composed, alternating, and input-conditioned transformations at the 6-8 ceiling
difficulty_levers: constant versus input-dependent or alternating rule
adaptive.notes: Sample a latent transformation, generate enough example pairs to identify it uniquely, and reject any item compatible with a simpler competing rule. Escalate on structural complexity rather than fact size, with unlimited parallel clones and a high procedural ceiling.

engagement_hook: Every correct prediction starts a whimsical machine whose gears spin and transform the incoming cargo into the expected output.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Children may infer an unintended rule from too few examples, so generation must test uniqueness against the full rule library. Animation timing cannot create a memory demand; all example pairs remain visible. Keep arithmetic facts easy, pair later numerals with magnitudes, avoid color-only conditions, use large tap targets, and never treat faster responding as better reasoning.

name: Balance Lab
topics_techniques_covered: balance_equivalence: choose or build figure weights that keep a two-pan scale level
number_sentence_building: complete a missing quantity so two visibly represented sides remain equal
number_properties_reasoning: use decomposition, substitution, and equal-group structure to infer hidden figure weights
quantitative_comparison: distinguish equal load from left-heavy and right-heavy configurations
one_liner: The child adds figure weights until both sides of a scale are exactly level.
interaction: One or more level example scales establish the weights of pictured shapes; a final scale has an empty outlined pan or hook. The child taps a candidate load or drags large figure weights from a tray onto the empty pan, can remove or rearrange them, and taps a balance button to submit. The beam moves continuously as a consequence cue, but scored correctness is revealed only after submission; no labels, typing, or written equations are required.
self_teach: A wordless ghost hand places one star beside another star on the empty pan; the tilted beam rises to level and glows, all within 10 seconds. One unscored warm-up asks the child to balance two circles with an obvious matching pair, supplying a gentle corrective placement before scored scales.

learning_science.principle: Conceptual knowledge of mathematical equivalence supports transferable solution procedures
learning_science.why: A level beam makes same-value-on-both-sides concrete and exposes whether the child reasons relationally rather than merely totals visible objects.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Score balance-preserving substitutions and decompositions, not just the final load, and progress from concrete equal sets to hidden figure values.
learning_science.source: Rittle-Johnson, B., & Alibali, M. W. (1999). Conceptual and procedural knowledge of mathematics: Does one lead to the other? Journal of Educational Psychology, 91(1), 175-189.

learning_science.principle: Early algebraic thinking grows from children's intuitive use of equality and properties of operations
learning_science.why: Replacing equal groups and decomposing a load can reveal generalized arithmetic reasoning without letters or equations.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Generated scales preserve simple substitution, commutative grouping, and decomposition structures while representing every unknown as a figure.
learning_science.source: Carpenter, T. P., Franke, M. L., & Levi, L. (2003). Thinking Mathematically: Integrating Arithmetic and Algebra in Elementary School. Heinemann.

learning_science.principle: Relational complexity, not surface size, should control the reasoning ceiling
learning_science.why: A multi-example scale becomes hard when several weight relations must be coordinated, even if every quantity is small.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Escalate from direct matching to chains of two, three, or four linked figure relations and key partial-credit states to constraints already satisfied.
learning_science.source: Halford, G. S., Wilson, W. H., & Phillips, S. (1998). Processing capacity defined by relational complexity. Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 21(6), 803-831.

tail_precision_rationale: M-POLY grades how many equivalence constraints the constructed load satisfies, and M-PATH plus M-PLANFUL distinguish substitution or decomposition from random add-remove search. M-ERRTYPE labels visual matching, object-counting, one-relation-only, and wrong-direction adjustments. Adaptive chains make M-DIFFREACH a direct estimate of the maximum number of linked equalities coordinated, while M-LEARNRATE captures rapid uptake of novel figure values; together these signals separate equally correct children at the gifted cut.
age_rationale: K-1 uses one two-pan scale, identical visible objects, small exact quantities, and large tap-to-add pieces, requiring no reading, number symbols, or precise dragging. Grades 2-3 infer one hidden figure weight from a level example; grades 4-5 chain substitutions; grades 6-8 coordinate several linked figure values and multiple valid decompositions. The concrete beam preserves meaning while formal equation notation remains absent.

adaptive.content_range: direct one-to-one balancing with identical concrete pieces at K-1 through multi-example substitution and decomposition problems with four linked figure weights at the 6-8 ceiling
difficulty_levers: number of example scales and linked figure types
direct match versus inferred hidden weights
presence of multiple valid-looking near balances
adaptive.notes: Generate integer latent weights first, derive level examples, and enumerate tray combinations to ensure at least one intended solution and misconception-keyed foils. The system can escalate relation count to a ceiling without increasing notation or reading demand.

engagement_hook: The laboratory beam reacts satisfyingly to every piece, and a perfect solution locks level with a bright equilibrium pulse.
construct_irrelevant_risks: A visibly larger shape must not imply greater weight unless deliberately established; randomize size and position independently of value. Beam animation should show direction without allowing endless feedback-based hill climbing on scored items. Provide large tap alternatives to drag, avoid color-only identity, keep all premises visible, and separate motor slips from reasoning through M-PATH and forgiving removal.

name: Hanging Mobile
topics_techniques_covered: balance_equivalence: preserve equilibrium across several connected arms of a hanging mobile
number_sentence_building: infer missing figure quantities from multiple linked equal-value constraints without symbolic equations
word_problem_reasoning: coordinate a multi-constraint quantitative system and propagate a solved relationship through the whole structure
one_liner: The child completes a hanging mobile so every arm stays level at once.
interaction: A multi-arm mobile shows several balanced branches and one empty hook; repeated figures have consistent hidden weights. The child taps a candidate cluster or drags figures from a large tray to the hook, can undo or rearrange, and taps the center hanger to submit. Arms respond visually after each placement but do not reveal the keyed solution until commit; all constraints remain on screen and no text, numerals, or algebra notation appears.
self_teach: In a wordless animation under 10 seconds, the ghost hand adds a matching moon to an empty lower hook; that arm levels, then the upper arm levels, and the whole mobile sparkles. One unscored two-arm warm-up follows, with a corrective ghost placement if the mobile remains tilted.

learning_science.principle: Relational complexity theory defines processing demand by how many independent relations must be integrated
learning_science.why: A hanging mobile naturally scales from one equality to a system in which lower-arm results constrain higher arms.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Difficulty is driven by branch depth, linked figure types, and simultaneous constraints rather than by large numbers or formal system notation.
learning_science.source: Halford, G. S., Wilson, W. H., & Phillips, S. (1998). Processing capacity defined by relational complexity. Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 21(6), 803-831.

learning_science.principle: Grounded external representations can make quantitative relations more comprehensible than formal symbols
learning_science.why: Level arms and repeated figures embody a system of equalities while removing algebra-reading demands.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Keep every premise visible in the physical mobile, use consistent figure identities, and let the child manipulate concrete clusters rather than solve written equations.
learning_science.source: Koedinger, K. R., & Nathan, M. J. (2004). The real story behind story problems: Effects of representations on quantitative reasoning. Journal of the Learning Sciences, 13(2), 129-164.

learning_science.principle: Cognitive load theory favors reducing extraneous search while preserving intrinsic relational demand
learning_science.why: Decorative motion or hidden premises would turn a systems problem into attention or memory noise.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Freeze nonessential sway, show the whole mobile at once, use a small organized tray, and increase only constraint depth and ambiguity.
learning_science.source: Sweller, J., van Merrienboer, J. J. G., & Paas, F. (2019). Cognitive architecture and instructional design: 20 years later. Educational Psychology Review, 31(2), 261-292.

tail_precision_rationale: M-POLY and M-PROG score how many lower and upper constraints are satisfied over time, so a nearly solved four-relation mobile contributes more information than a binary miss. M-PATH and M-PLANFUL reveal whether the child solves from constrained leaves upward, substitutes systematically, or guesses clusters. M-DIFFREACH marks maximum branch depth and linked-relation count, while M-LEARNRATE captures acceleration across novel mobile structures; this process-rich evidence sharpens decisions among high performers who all solve simpler balances.
age_rationale: The type starts at grades 2-3 because even the entry item requires coordinating a lower balance with its effect on a parent arm; K-1 is served by the single-scale Balance Lab. Grades 2-3 use two levels and two figure types, grades 4-5 add substitution chains, and grades 6-8 use deeper asymmetric mobiles with redundant or minimally sufficient clues. Large hooks, tap-to-place alternatives, and zero text remove reading and fine-motor barriers.

adaptive.content_range: two-level mobiles with direct repeated-figure equivalence through deep multi-branch systems requiring chained substitution, decomposition, and consistency across four or more constraints
difficulty_levers: mobile depth and number of branches
number of distinct hidden figure weights
adaptive.notes: Generate latent integer figure weights and a balanced tree, mask one load, then enumerate candidate completions and solution paths. Partial states are automatically scoreable by satisfied branches, enabling procedural adaptation to repeated failure at a relation-count ceiling.

engagement_hook: Completing the mobile triggers a cascading level-up from the lowest arm to the top, ending in a gentle kinetic sculpture animation.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Motion can distract or induce visual tracking demands, so mobiles settle immediately during reasoning and animate only on feedback. Shape size, branch length, and color must not leak weight unless explicitly controlled; color is never the sole identity cue. Keep premises visible, offer tap placement for motor accessibility, and prevent scored trial-and-error by withholding exact balance feedback until submit.

name: Number Line Jump
topics_techniques_covered: number_sense_magnitude: place whole quantities, grouped quantities, and visually represented rational parts on bounded number lines
number_sense_magnitude: estimate location on sparse or unmarked scales and transfer magnitude across changing ranges
quantitative_comparison: compare a target with anchors, midpoints, and intervals to decide where it belongs
one_liner: The child slides a jumper to the place on a line that matches a shown quantity.
interaction: A horizontal bounded line shows two endpoints and, when appropriate, a few anchor marks; above it sits a target rendered as dots, grouped blocks, a shaded fraction strip, or a numeral paired with that visual. The child drags a large jumper or moves it with a coarse slider, releases at the chosen location, and taps GO. K-1 sees dot quantities on a short partitioned line and never types or reads numerals.
self_teach: A wordless ghost hand counts a five-dot target, slides the jumper halfway along a ten-step line, and taps GO; the jumper lands with a soft glow in under 10 seconds. One unscored placement warm-up follows on a fully ticked line, showing the correct landing if the release is outside the broad target zone.

learning_science.principle: Number-line estimation reveals changing internal representations of numerical magnitude
learning_science.why: Placement patterns distinguish compressed from increasingly linear mappings and provide more information than a larger-smaller choice.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Collect continuous placement error across ranges and progressively remove ticks while preserving clear endpoints.
learning_science.source: Siegler, R. S., & Opfer, J. E. (2003). The development of numerical estimation: Evidence for multiple representations of numerical quantity. Psychological Science, 14(3), 237-250.

learning_science.principle: Young children's number-line estimates develop measurably from kindergarten through the early grades
learning_science.why: K-1 can participate when quantities are concrete and the scale is short, while later bands can tolerate sparse anchors and wider ranges.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Start with dot targets and fully partitioned 0-to-10-like lines, then fade partitions and expand to whole and visually represented rational magnitudes.
learning_science.source: Siegler, R. S., & Booth, J. L. (2004). Development of numerical estimation in young children. Child Development, 75(2), 428-444.

learning_science.principle: A central conceptual structure links counting, quantity, and ordered magnitude
learning_science.why: Representing the same value as objects, groups, and a location tests integrated number sense rather than isolated symbol knowledge.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Cross representation forms within the adaptive run while pairing any numeral with a magnitude model, so transfer among quantity and space is observable.
learning_science.source: Case, R., & Griffin, S. (1990). Child cognitive development: The role of central conceptual structures in the development of scientific and social thought. In C.-A. Hauert (Ed.), Developmental Psychology: Cognitive, Perceptuo-Motor, and Neurological Perspectives, 193-230. North-Holland.

tail_precision_rationale: M-PAE turns every release into a continuous error measure and supports a placement curve, preserving fine differences when broad correctness bands would ceiling. M-CONSIST across matched values and representation forms distinguishes stable magnitude knowledge from lucky placements. M-DIFFREACH records the sparsest anchors, widest range, and most complex rational representation accurately placed, while M-LEARNRATE tracks improvement as scaffolding fades; M-ACC supplies tolerance-banded evidence for adaptive routing.
age_rationale: K-1 uses short fully partitioned lines, dot targets, a large thumb, and broad zones, avoiding numeral reading and precision motor demands. Grades 2-3 use grouped tens and fading ticks; grades 4-5 add wide ranges and visual fraction strips; grades 6-8 place equivalent ratios, decimals, or signed offsets shown through visual models rather than requiring notation fluency. Slider and tap-nudge alternatives support children who cannot drag precisely.

adaptive.content_range: small dot quantities on fully ticked lines at K-1 through sparse-anchor placement of large, fractional, decimal, ratio, and signed magnitudes represented visually at the 6-8 ceiling
difficulty_levers: tick density and number of labeled anchors
target distance from familiar anchors or midpoint
whole versus grouped versus rational representation
adaptive.notes: Targets and scales are procedurally sampled with edge, midpoint, and interior coverage; score continuously with M-PAE and adapt tolerance, range, and anchor sparsity. Parallel forms can use equivalent visual targets at different scales, creating a high ceiling without adding prose.

engagement_hook: The marker is a tiny jumper that springs to the selected landing spot, with longer and stranger number landscapes unlocking as accuracy grows.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Drag precision, screen size, and parallax can inflate placement error; use a thick line, large thumb, tap-nudge controls, device calibration, and error normalized by range. Endpoint labels and fraction symbols cannot be prerequisites for young children. Keep spatial length fixed across comparison items when needed, avoid decorative landmarks that cue answers, and do not reward raw speed.

name: More or Fewer
topics_techniques_covered: number_sense_magnitude: approximate number system comparison of briefly shown dot arrays without counting
number_sense_magnitude: discriminate progressively closer quantity ratios across varied dot layouts
quantitative_comparison: choose which of two nonsymbolic sets contains more while ignoring nonnumeric visual cues
one_liner: The child taps the side that flashed more dots.
interaction: Two dot clouds appear simultaneously for a brief calibrated exposure, disappear behind neutral covers, and leave two large side buttons. The child taps the side that had more; no numerals, words, dragging, or counting response is required. Array ratio adapts while dot size, density, total area, convex hull, and color relationships are counterbalanced.
self_teach: In a wordless animation under 10 seconds, three large dots and eight large dots flash, the ghost hand taps the eight-dot side, and that cover opens to show the larger group. One unscored easy-ratio warm-up follows with a replay and corrective highlight if needed before the timed scored flashes.

learning_science.principle: Individual differences in nonsymbolic number acuity can be estimated from ratio-dependent discrimination
learning_science.why: A psychometric staircase over close quantity ratios yields a low-literacy continuous measure rather than relying on learned numeral knowledge.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Adapt the ratio of the two arrays and fit accuracy by ratio to estimate M-WEBER rather than treating all comparisons as equally difficult.
learning_science.source: Halberda, J., Mazzocco, M. M. M., & Feigenson, L. (2008). Individual differences in non-verbal number acuity correlate with maths achievement. Nature, 455, 665-668.

learning_science.principle: Continuous visual properties can influence nonsymbolic number judgments
learning_science.why: If area, density, dot size, or convex hull consistently covaries with count, the task measures perceptual shortcuts rather than numerical discrimination.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Generate incongruent and cue-balanced trials across multiple visual dimensions, log cue condition, and estimate acuity only from a balanced set.
learning_science.source: Gebuis, T., & Reynvoet, B. (2012). The interplay between nonsymbolic number and its continuous visual properties. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 141(4), 642-648.

learning_science.principle: Cognitive load theory supports a minimal interface when a brief perceptual representation is the target
learning_science.why: Instructions, decorative motion, or complex response mapping would consume attention unrelated to approximate magnitude.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use one stable left-right response, a wordless example, neutral covers, and no concurrent animation or text during exposure.
learning_science.source: Sweller, J., van Merrienboer, J. J. G., & Paas, F. (2019). Cognitive architecture and instructional design: 20 years later. Educational Psychology Review, 31(2), 261-292.

tail_precision_rationale: M-WEBER is the primary tail statistic: a fitted threshold estimates the finest ratio the child reliably discriminates and remains continuous when easy arrays ceiling. M-DIFFREACH records the closest ratio solved under cue-balanced conditions, and M-CONSIST guards against side-biased or noisy estimates. M-RT and M-SPEEDACC are interpreted only with accuracy so impulsive fast taps receive no advantage, while M-ACC across many balanced trials anchors the psychometric fit.
age_rationale: The task is deliberately limited to K-1 and grades 2-3, where a preliteracy, notation-free magnitude signal is most valuable. Both bands use one large left-right tap and no fine motor action; K-1 begins with long exposures and wide ratios, while grades 2-3 receive shorter flashes and closer ratios. Older bands are better served by symbolic and relational quantitative types rather than extending this narrow perceptual construct.

adaptive.content_range: large-ratio comparisons with small arrays and generous exposure through close-ratio, larger-array, brief-exposure comparisons under incongruent continuous visual cues
difficulty_levers: distance from the child's fitted threshold
adaptive.notes: Use a constrained dot-array generator that balances several continuous visual features across count and reject arrays with overlap or obvious subgroups. A staircase concentrates trials near the estimated Weber threshold, but a sufficient spread of ratios and cue conditions is retained for a stable fit.

engagement_hook: Two firefly swarms flash past and the child quickly chooses the bigger swarm, with closer contests appearing as their detector sharpens.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Area, density, dot size, convex hull, brightness, clustering, and side preference are major confounds and must be counterbalanced jointly, not one at a time. Exposure must be frame-timed across devices and long enough for visual access but short enough to discourage counting. Screen glare, visual impairment, and color vision require high-contrast achromatic defaults; raw speed is never scored without accuracy.

name: Story Graph
topics_techniques_covered: word_problem_reasoning: model two growing quantities and identify when one catches, exceeds, or equals the other
word_problem_reasoning: connect an animated quantity story to height, bar, line, and accumulated-total representations
proportional_reasoning: compare constant and changing rates through steepness, equal intervals, and covariation
quantitative_reasoning_mixed: reason from simple graph height through rate-of-change and area-as-accumulation ideas without calculus notation
one_liner: The child makes or chooses the graph that tells the same growing-quantity story as an animation.
interaction: A short silent animation shows one or two quantities changing over equal visual time steps - for example tanks filling or creatures moving - beside a graph with icon axes and no prose. Depending on level, the child taps the matching bar or curve, drags points to complete a path, slides an equality marker to where two paths meet, or stacks rate strips under a timeline to predict the accumulated height, then taps GO. Values use pictorial units or optional magnitude bars; no formulas or typed answers appear.
self_teach: In a wordless demo under 10 seconds, a tank rises one block at each beat while a ghost hand raises successive graph points one block, then taps the matching line and both glow together. One unscored warm-up asks the child to match a two-step rising bar story, replaying the animation and showing the correspondence after an error.

learning_science.principle: Graph sense develops through coordinated attention to graph purpose, task, display structure, and reader knowledge
learning_science.why: A child can read a height yet fail to infer a trend or relation, so the type must deliberately progress across levels of graph comprehension.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Sequence items from direct height and bar matching to between-point trend, comparison of two paths, rate, and accumulation, keeping axes and story semantics stable.
learning_science.source: Friel, S. N., Curcio, F. R., & Bright, G. W. (2001). Making sense of graphs: Critical factors influencing comprehension and instructional implications. Journal for Research in Mathematics Education, 32(2), 124-158.

learning_science.principle: Covariational reasoning involves coordinating how one quantity changes in tandem with another
learning_science.why: Slope and changing-rate reasoning should emerge from dynamic co-change, not from memorized graph vocabulary.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Animate equal time steps in lockstep with graph construction and escalate from amount change to rate change and accumulation while avoiding derivative notation.
learning_science.source: Carlson, M. P., Jacobs, S., Coe, E., Larsen, S., & Hsu, E. (2002). Applying covariational reasoning while modeling dynamic events: A framework and a study. Journal for Research in Mathematics Education, 33(5), 352-378.

learning_science.principle: Grounded representations can make quantitative relations easier to comprehend than equivalent formal symbolism
learning_science.why: A filling tank or moving object provides semantic meaning for height, steepness, intersection, and accumulated total.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Every graph is linked to a replayable visual event, with icons and synchronized beats replacing written scenarios and formulas.
learning_science.source: Koedinger, K. R., & Nathan, M. J. (2004). The real story behind story problems: Effects of representations on quantitative reasoning. Journal of the Learning Sciences, 13(2), 129-164.

tail_precision_rationale: M-POLY scores separately whether a construction preserves starting amount, direction, relative steepness, intersection, and final accumulation. M-PATH and M-PLANFUL reveal whether the child coordinates points in temporal order or patches the curve by visual guessing, while M-ERRTYPE distinguishes height-rate, slope-level, intersection, and accumulation confusions. M-DIFFREACH marks the deepest graph idea solved and M-LEARNRATE tracks movement from story matching to novel changing-rate and accumulation cases, giving substantially more tail resolution than a single graph-reading item.
age_rationale: The type begins at grades 2-3 because even icon axes require coordinating two ordered dimensions; entry items use large discrete bars and one changing quantity. Grades 4-5 add two lines, equal time beats, rate comparison, and intersections; grades 6-8 add changing rates and accumulation from visible rate strips without calculus symbols. Replayable animation removes reading and memory barriers, while tap and coarse drag controls avoid precision drawing.

adaptive.content_range: direct matching of discrete heights or bars to a short visual story through two-quantity covariation, intersections, changing steepness, and qualitative accumulation from rate strips
difficulty_levers: number of time intervals and turning points
direct match versus prediction or construction
height, intersection, slope, and accumulation relation count
adaptive.notes: Generate a latent piecewise quantity story, derive animation frames and graph coordinates from the same data, and produce foils by named graph misconceptions. Escalation can independently vary representation and relation depth while preserving a wordless, procedurally cloneable shell.

engagement_hook: The child is a story cartographer: graph paths visibly drive races, filling tanks, and growing towers, so a correct model makes the animation and graph move in perfect sync.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Prior graph instruction and axis conventions can dominate unless the synchronized demo establishes the mapping; use icons, equal beats, and no vocabulary. Animation must be replayable so working memory is not the hidden test. Avoid color-only line identity, cramped point dragging, misleading aspect ratios, decorative motion, and scales that make slope comparisons visually deceptive.

name: Fair Share
topics_techniques_covered: proportional_reasoning: preserve an ingredient ratio while scaling a mixture up, down, or to a non-integer multiple
proportional_reasoning: unitize, compose equivalent ratios, and distinguish multiplicative scaling from constant-difference adjustment
number_sense_magnitude: compare relative amounts of two ingredient quantities rather than absolute totals
quantitative_comparison: judge which candidate mixture has the same concentration or fair-share structure
one_liner: The child changes two ingredient amounts so the new mix keeps the same taste.
interaction: A target bowl displays two kinds of tokens in a clear part-to-part arrangement; beside it, a larger or smaller bowl has one or both ingredient rows incomplete. The child taps plus-minus scoops or drags whole token groups into the second bowl, then taps a taste button to submit. Ratio is encoded by shape and texture as well as color, quantities remain countable or grouped, and no recipe text, fraction notation, or typed numerals are used.
self_teach: A wordless ghost hand copies one berry and two drops into a second bowl, then adds another full one-to-two batch; both bowls show the same happy taste face, all in under 10 seconds. One unscored doubling warm-up follows, and an additive-error attempt receives a corrective animation that adds a complete batch before scoring begins.

learning_science.principle: Proportional reasoning depends on unitizing, relative thinking, covariation, and reasoning up and down
learning_science.why: Keeping a mix invariant requires coordinating two quantities multiplicatively rather than applying the same additive change to each.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Items progress from whole-number replication of a visible composite unit to shrinking, non-doubling, missing-part, and comparison cases, while logging multiplicative versus additive moves.
learning_science.source: Lamon, S. J. (2007). Rational numbers and proportional reasoning: Toward a theoretical framework. In F. K. Lester (Ed.), Second Handbook of Research on Mathematics Teaching and Learning, 629-668. Information Age Publishing.

learning_science.principle: Grounded representations can elicit meaningful quantitative strategies before formal ratio symbolism is mastered
learning_science.why: Ingredient groups make the invariant relation visible and let a child reason proportionally without cross-products or fraction notation.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Use manipulable token batches and visual grouping, introduce no written ratio, and test transfer to new totals and layouts.
learning_science.source: Koedinger, K. R., & Nathan, M. J. (2004). The real story behind story problems: Effects of representations on quantitative reasoning. Journal of the Learning Sciences, 13(2), 129-164.

learning_science.principle: Learning trajectories support adaptive movement from concrete composite units to generalized multiplicative relations
learning_science.why: Younger children can replicate a batch before they can coordinate less obvious scale factors.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Route from repeated whole batches to missing-value, shrink, comparison, and fractional-batch visual cases based on observed strategy and accuracy.
learning_science.source: Clements, D. H., & Sarama, J. (2004). Learning trajectories in mathematics education. Mathematical Thinking and Learning, 6(2), 81-89.

tail_precision_rationale: M-PROPSTRAT directly classifies multiplicative scaling versus the tempting constant-difference strategy, so a correct lucky endpoint and a consistently proportional construction are not equivalent. M-PATH and M-PLANFUL expose complete-batch replication, unitizing, and systematic adjustment, while M-POLY credits one correctly scaled ingredient or an equivalent intermediate batch. M-DIFFREACH identifies the hardest scale factor and representation handled, and M-LEARNRATE shows how rapidly strategy becomes multiplicative across unfamiliar mixes.
age_rationale: Grades 2-3 begin with small countable whole batches and simple doubling or fair sharing; the task is not assigned to K-1 because coordinating two varying quantities is not assumed. Grades 4-5 add missing parts, shrinking, and non-doubling whole-number scales; grades 6-8 add comparison, inverse, and visually represented fractional scale factors. Large scoops, grouped tokens, and no text or ratio notation minimize motor, reading, and symbolic demands.

adaptive.content_range: copying and doubling a small visible composite unit through missing-value, shrink, non-integer scale, inverse, and concentration-comparison problems
difficulty_levers: scale factor from whole to visually represented fractional
target total size and availability of a composite-unit cue
adaptive.notes: Generate coprime base ratios and valid scaled mixtures, reject ambiguous displays, and derive additive and one-component foils automatically. The move log supports strategy-aware routing: children using additive changes receive a diagnostic parallel item, while consistent multiplicative solvers escalate to a ceiling.

engagement_hook: The child is a tiny flavor scientist; preserving the mix earns a delighted taste reaction and fills a recipe shelf with increasingly unusual visual ingredients.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Blended color or a taste-face preview could turn the task into perceptual matching, so the outcome appears only after submission and ratio is represented by countable textured shapes. Color is never the sole ingredient cue. Keep counting load modest, offer tap scoops instead of precise dragging, avoid culturally specific foods, and distinguish motor corrections from strategic revisions.

name: Make It Equal
topics_techniques_covered: number_sentence_building: solve mathematical-equivalence forms such as 3+4=_+5 by making both sides the same amount
number_sentence_building: complete non-canonical open equations with the unknown in varied positions and operations on both sides
balance_equivalence: interpret the equal sign relationally as two equal quantities rather than an instruction to produce a total
one_liner: The child places the missing quantity that makes both sides of the equal sign match.
interaction: Two sides appear around a large equal sign, each backed by a faint two-pan balance; quantities are dot groups or numeral-plus-bar tiles and joining or removing is shown with simple action icons. One side has a snap slot. The child taps or drags one of 4-6 quantity tiles into the slot and taps GO; no numeral typing, reading, or algebraic variable is required.
self_teach: In a wordless animation under 10 seconds, three dots join four dots on the left while two dots join an empty slot on the right; the ghost hand inserts five dots, both quantity bars become equal length, and the equal sign glows. One unscored non-canonical warm-up follows with a corrective balance animation before scored equations.

learning_science.principle: Equal-sign knowledge is context-sensitive and children often interpret equals operationally rather than relationally
learning_science.why: Canonical answer-after-equals formats can hide a misconception that fails when operations appear on both sides.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Most items use non-canonical structures, vary the unknown position, and include distractors corresponding to adding every visible quantity or writing a left-side total.
learning_science.source: McNeil, N. M., & Alibali, M. W. (2005). Knowledge change as a function of mathematics experience: All contexts are not created equal. Journal of Cognition and Development, 6(2), 285-306.

learning_science.principle: Conceptual understanding of equivalence can support procedural transfer
learning_science.why: Seeing both sides as the same amount is more general than memorizing a single missing-number procedure.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Pair dot groups and length bars with varied equation forms, then fade some concrete support while retaining the relational balance cue.
learning_science.source: Rittle-Johnson, B., & Alibali, M. W. (1999). Conceptual and procedural knowledge of mathematics: Does one lead to the other? Journal of Educational Psychology, 91(1), 175-189.

learning_science.principle: Arithmetic and early algebra can be integrated through relational thinking about equality and operation properties
learning_science.why: Commuting, decomposing, and compensating quantities reveal algebra-ready structure without letter symbols.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Escalate from direct matching to compensation, decomposition, repeated groups, and equivalence transformations while keeping values visually grounded.
learning_science.source: Carpenter, T. P., Franke, M. L., & Levi, L. (2003). Thinking Mathematically: Integrating Arithmetic and Algebra in Elementary School. Heinemann.

tail_precision_rationale: M-EQREL uses the first substantive choice to distinguish a relational solution from operational total-all or answer-after-equals signatures. M-ERRTYPE preserves compensation, inverse-operation, side-confusion, and near-miss evidence, while M-REV records spontaneous correction before commit without requiring an explanation. M-DIFFREACH marks the most structurally non-canonical equivalence handled and M-LEARNRATE captures transfer as concrete bars fade, sharpening tail placement beyond arithmetic accuracy alone.
age_rationale: The type begins at grades 2-3 because the equal and join/remove symbols are the minimal notation being assessed; dot groups, bars, and the balance backdrop prevent reading or numeral fluency from being prerequisites. Grades 4-5 add varied unknown positions and operations on both sides; grades 6-8 add compensation, repeated groups, and nested visual operations without letters. All responses use large tiles, never typed numerals.

adaptive.content_range: small dot-group non-canonical equalities through multi-operation compensation, decomposition, repeated-group, and unknown-position equivalence structures
difficulty_levers: one versus multiple operations across both sides
concrete quantity support and degree of fading
compensation, decomposition, inverse, or repeated-group structure
adaptive.notes: Generate two equal expression trees, mask one leaf or group, and produce distractors from documented operational strategies. Strategy-aware adaptation samples parallel forms to confirm M-EQREL before escalating structural depth, keeping arithmetic values small relative to the equivalence demand.

engagement_hook: Every solved equality steadies a glowing bridge between two islands, making same-on-both-sides physically satisfying.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Prior worksheet format can bias children toward operational responding; varied layouts and the wordless relational demo mitigate familiarity without coaching scored answers. Arithmetic fact difficulty must remain below structural difficulty, and bars must not directly reveal an answer option through pixel matching. Use texture plus color, large snap slots, no time bonus, and log accidental swaps separately from conceptual revisions.

name: Biggest Number
topics_techniques_covered: number_properties_reasoning: arrange quantity or digit tiles to create the largest or smallest possible value
number_properties_reasoning: satisfy visual even-odd, equal-group factor, divisibility, and multi-constraint conditions while optimizing value
number_sense_magnitude: compose and compare place-value quantities using ones, groups, and positional magnitude
quantitative_comparison: reason about which placement or swap increases, decreases, or preserves the constructed value
one_liner: The child rearranges quantity tiles to build the biggest or smallest value that obeys the pictured rules.
interaction: A row of large cards and ordered place slots appears beside a goal icon: a tall mountain for largest or a small burrow for smallest. The child drags cards into slots or taps a card then a slot, can swap freely, and taps GO. K-1 cards are dot towers placed into two magnitude lanes; later bands use digit cards paired with place-value blocks, while pair icons and equal-group trays convey even-odd or factor constraints without words or typed input.
self_teach: In a wordless demo under 10 seconds, the ghost hand swaps a larger dot tower into the left high-value lane; the built magnitude bar grows and the mountain glows. One unscored two-card warm-up follows, and if reversed, the bars compare and the hand demonstrates the better swap before scoring.

learning_science.principle: Number sense develops through an integrated structure linking quantity, counting, comparison, and place value
learning_science.why: Optimization is meaningful only when the child understands that a card's position changes its contribution to the whole.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Begin with visible quantity lanes, pair later digit positions with base-unit blocks, and fade those supports as place-value reasoning stabilizes.
learning_science.source: Case, R., & Griffin, S. (1990). Child cognitive development: The role of central conceptual structures in the development of scientific and social thought. In C.-A. Hauert (Ed.), Developmental Psychology: Cognitive, Perceptuo-Motor, and Neurological Perspectives, 193-230. North-Holland.

learning_science.principle: Learning trajectories organize increasingly sophisticated mathematical actions around a stable goal
learning_science.why: The same arrange-and-compare shell can progress from direct magnitude to positional value and interacting number constraints.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Route from two concrete quantities to multi-place optimization, then add one and later several visually demonstrated property constraints.
learning_science.source: Clements, D. H., & Sarama, J. (2004). Learning trajectories in mathematics education. Mathematical Thinking and Learning, 6(2), 81-89.

learning_science.principle: Overlapping-waves theory highlights diverse strategies and increasingly adaptive choice among them
learning_science.why: Children may exhaustively try arrangements, place the largest card first, reason from the units constraint backward, or coordinate all constraints.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Log the full swap path and score systematic constraint-first or place-value-first planning against redundant trial-and-error.
learning_science.source: Siegler, R. S. (1996). Emerging Minds: The Process of Change in Children's Thinking. Oxford University Press.

tail_precision_rationale: M-PATH and M-PLANFUL reveal whether the child prioritizes the most valuable slot, satisfies a restrictive units condition first, and avoids redundant permutations. M-EFF compares the swap sequence with an optimal construction path, while M-ERRTYPE distinguishes reversed place value, local-greedy, parity, factor, and missed-constraint solutions. M-DIFFREACH records maximum slots and simultaneous properties coordinated, and M-LEARNRATE captures rapid strategy improvement as new pictorial constraints are introduced.
age_rationale: K-1 uses two countable dot towers and two visually unequal place lanes, so no digit reading, property vocabulary, or precise dragging is needed. Grades 2-3 add two- and three-place digit cards with base-unit overlays and a pictured pair/no-leftover condition; grades 4-5 add several cards and one factor or parity constraint; grades 6-8 coordinate largest-smallest goals with multiple divisibility or equal-group constraints. Tap-then-slot is always available as a motor alternative.

adaptive.content_range: ordering two concrete quantities at K-1 through optimizing multi-place values under interacting parity, equal-group factor, divisibility, repetition, or fixed-position constraints
difficulty_levers: number of cards and place slots
largest versus smallest or bounded-target goal
quantity cards versus digits with fading place-value support
number of feasible arrangements and proximity of the runner-up
adaptive.notes: Enumerate all card permutations under generated constraints to guarantee a unique optimum or explicitly score ties. Create misconception-keyed near-optimal foils and adapt by slot count, support fading, and constraint count rather than by obscure number facts.

engagement_hook: The constructed value becomes a tower: smart swaps make it shoot upward toward the mountain or shrink neatly into the burrow while rule badges click into place.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Digit recognition and learned divisibility rules can become a knowledge barrier, so early items use quantity overlays and every property icon is self-taught through concrete pairs or equal groups. Do not use reading, color-only constraints, or tiny drag slots. Ensure animation does not expose the optimum before submission, keep search spaces age-appropriate, and treat repeated exploratory swaps as process evidence rather than a motor penalty.

name: Story Model
topics_techniques_covered: word_problem_reasoning: build a manipulable situation model for join, separate, compare, equal-group, sharing, and multi-step quantity stories
arithmetic_reasoning: derive an unknown quantity from pictured actions and relations without relying on written operation notation
quantitative_reasoning_mixed: coordinate quantities, unknown position, grouping, comparison, and multiple constraints in a visual story
one_liner: The child rebuilds a silent quantity story with objects or bars and uses the model to find what is missing.
interaction: A brief replayable animation shows objects joining, leaving, being compared, grouped, or shared; the final state contains a glowing question space. The child drags or tap-places objects and resizable unit bars into a model area, then taps the resulting quantity tile and GO. All story details are conveyed by motion and icons, every quantity remains visible on replay, and no prose, operation string, explanation, or typed numeral is required.
self_teach: In a wordless demo under 10 seconds, two birds land beside three birds; the ghost hand places matching two- and three-unit bars end to end, taps the five-object result, and both story and model glow. One unscored join warm-up follows with an unlimited replay and a corrective model-build animation after an error.

learning_science.principle: Solving arithmetic stories depends on constructing a situation model of the quantitative relations
learning_science.why: Keyword matching is insufficient when the unknown changes position or several relations interact.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Score the child's intermediate object or bar model, vary semantic schemas and unknown positions, and keep the animation replayable so comprehension can be separated from memory.
learning_science.source: Kintsch, W., & Greeno, J. G. (1985). Understanding and solving word arithmetic problems. Psychological Review, 92(1), 109-129.

learning_science.principle: Grounded representations can support quantitative reasoning when formal equations are harder to comprehend
learning_science.why: Objects, actions, and bars let children express relation structure without translating into algebraic notation.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Require model construction before answer selection and escalate relational depth while avoiding written equations or operation vocabulary.
learning_science.source: Koedinger, K. R., & Nathan, M. J. (2004). The real story behind story problems: Effects of representations on quantitative reasoning. Journal of the Learning Sciences, 13(2), 129-164.

learning_science.principle: Cognitively guided instruction research shows that children's strategies vary systematically with problem structure
learning_science.why: Join, separate, part-whole, compare, equal-group, and sharing situations elicit different valid models and reveal reasoning beyond a final answer.
learning_science.concrete_decision: Generate across semantic problem classes and score model structure and path, allowing multiple mathematically valid strategies rather than enforcing one operation sequence.
learning_science.source: Carpenter, T. P., Fennema, E., Franke, M. L., Levi, L., & Empson, S. B. (1999). Children's Mathematics: Cognitively Guided Instruction. Heinemann.

tail_precision_rationale: M-POLY grades whether the model captures the entities, grouping, direction of change, comparison relation, and final answer even when one component is wrong. M-PATH, M-PROG, and M-PLANFUL distinguish direct situation modeling, systematic bar construction, and useful decomposition from answer guessing or unstructured manipulation. M-DIFFREACH records the deepest semantic and multistep structure solved, while M-LEARNRATE tracks transfer across unfamiliar visual stories, yielding tail information that a written word-problem score would lose to reading variance.
age_rationale: The type begins at grades 2-3 because preserving a story relation while constructing a separate model requires more coordination than the K-1 catalog should assume, even with no reading. Grades 2-3 use one-step join, separate, compare, or equal-group animations with small quantities; grades 4-5 vary unknown position and add two steps; grades 6-8 coordinate nested groups, rates, remainders, and multiple constraints through bars and objects. Replay, large pieces, and tap placement reduce memory and motor demands.

adaptive.content_range: one-step concrete join, separate, compare, grouping, and sharing situations through multi-step, unknown-first, nested-group, rate, remainder, and multi-constraint visual models
difficulty_levers: number of sequential or nested relations
object model versus more compressed bar model
number of valid intermediate strategies and constraint interactions
adaptive.notes: Generate a latent situation graph first, render it as animation and manipulatives, and solve the graph to validate all accepted models and answers. Strategy-aware adaptation samples new semantic shells rather than merely larger numbers, with partial states automatically scored and replay available throughout.

engagement_hook: Tiny animated stories pause at a mystery moment, and the child becomes the scene builder whose model makes the ending play out.
construct_irrelevant_risks: Animation comprehension, cultural familiarity, and working memory can contaminate quantitative reasoning; use universal objects and actions, no speech or text, unlimited replay, and stable camera framing. Avoid irrelevant decorative characters, color-only grouping, tiny pieces, and story timing pressure. Multiple valid models must receive equal credit, and quantities should stay easy enough that relational modeling - not fact recall - sets difficulty.
